newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Malian mediator presses for four-day Bangui truce.
newsitem.headline: Malian mediator presses for four-day Bangui truce.

text.p: Malian mediator Amadou Toumani Toure proposed a four-day truce in the Central African Republic capital on Friday as the city enjoyed a day of calm after a week of clashes between African peacekeepers and army dissidents.

At the same time, the army dissidents, who staged three army mutinies in under a year and have yet to rejoin their units under a January peace deal, handed in several mortars without their sights to France's ambassador as gesture of goodwill.
But efforts to persuade the ex-mutineers to agree the truce were not immediately successful.

Toumani Toure, Mali's widely respected former military leader who negotiated the January deal, said the truce would permit families to bury their dead and the ex-mutineers to hand over all their heavy weapons.
"The handover of heavy weapons must take place during the truce," he told Reuters.
Calm returned to the battered city on Thursday afternoon. It has been calm since then.

The Red Cross says that the clashes, which began on June 20 after an incident involving peacekeepers and mutineers who had yet to rejoin their units, has killed 80 people, mostly civilians, and wounded 150.
The U.N. refugee agency says more than 50,000 civilians have fled their homes and need emergency shelter and food.

Mutinies in April and May 1996 began as pay protests but evolved into a bid to topple President Ange-Felix Patasse, a civilian from the north, elected in 1993. A third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.
Most of the mutineers are members of the Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.

Former colonial power France, which has troops in the country under a defence pact, intervened in support of the peacekeepers and one of its helicopters hit mortar batteries manned by dissident soldiers after its embassy came under fire.
Five French nationals in the embassy compound were among scores of people injured in the fighting.
French troops intervened directly to stop fighting in January before handing over to the African peacekeeping force.

Toumani Toure, who steered his West African country to democracy in 1992 after toppling dictator Moussa Traore, has repeatedly said Central African Republic citizens must solve the problem among themselves and no-one can do it for them.
He plans to hold talks with Patasse on Saturday.
Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo have troops in the 800-strong force. Patasse opponents criticise the Chadians, saying Patasse hired Chadians in a private militia.
